title: Dusk as a practice
hook: lamps lit, work put down, the family gathered

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ardas, and your line, stand at day's end. Did you stand for a moment and widen it to everyone? Today, not a text, but a time of day. Day four hundred eighteen.

Your phone probably knows when the sun sets. Around dusk the screen goes a little warmer, a little dimmer, without you asking. Somebody decided our devices should notice the evening. It's easy not to. A day can go straight from the last meeting to the commute to dinner to scrolling in bed, and never quite end; it just runs out. Long before screens, Punjabi households had a way to make the evening a real turning point. Today: dusk as a practice.
screen: `YOUR PHONE NOTICES SUNSET.` → `IT'S EASY NOT TO.` → `THE DAY DOESN'T END; IT RUNS OUT.`

segments.voice: The old Punjabi word is sandhiaa. It comes from a root meaning a joining: the seam where day and night meet. In South Asia, households of more than one faith mark that seam. Lamps are lit. Shoes come off. Work is put down. Hindu neighbors keep sandhya prayers too, and in Punjabi homes, Sikh and Hindu, a small lamp at dusk has been an ordinary sight. For Sikhs, dusk is when Rehras is said. The Sikh code of conduct places it in the evening, after sunset. Notice how that's put. Not to the minute. In the evening, as the light goes. The Gurus questioned rituals kept for their own sake, and gurbani puts remembrance above outward observance. So the lamp isn't the prayer. It's a reminder that the prayer is due. What makes dusk a practice, then, is the putting down. The shop shutter comes down. The laptop closes. The family, or just you, gathers. The day is handed back. Sikh life asks for kirat karni, honest work, through the day, and sandhiaa is the moment that work is allowed to stop. That's the gift of a seam. Without it, today bleeds into tonight and tonight into tomorrow, and nothing is ever finished. With it, the day can actually end. Put the day down.
screen: `SANDHIAA: THE SEAM OF DAY AND NIGHT.` · `LAMPS LIT, SHOES OFF, WORK DOWN.` · `REHRAS IN THE EVENING, AFTER SUNSET.` · `THE LAMP REMINDS; REMEMBRANCE PRAYS.` · then, large: `PUT THE DAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light one lamp at dusk. If you can, light a candle or a small lamp now, or just switch on one warm light and turn off the overhead. If it isn't dusk yet, plan where you'll do it tonight. Look at the light. Then name, silently, one piece of today's work you are putting down: the email, the argument, the unfinished task. Picture setting it on a shelf till morning. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, and let that be the evening beginning. The bell holds the time.
Sandhiaa. Dusk, the joining of day and night, when Sikhs say Rehras: lamps lit, work put down, the household gathered.
Your line: put the day down. Tonight, choose one moment, a shutter, a closed laptop, a lit lamp, that says the workday is over, and keep it. Day four hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs say Rehras Sahib in the evening, after sunset, and some households mark dusk by putting work down, lighting a lamp and gathering, though the remembrance, not the lamp, is the heart of it.
